title: The second generation
hookLine: children grow up with Punjabi at home, other languages outside, and Gurmukhi classes at weekends

cards: Saturday morning, a gurdwara in Toronto, or Leicester, or Melbourne, or California.
In a side room, a dozen kids sit at folding tables with notebooks, tracing curly letters while a patient teacher says each sound out loud. They'd rather be asleep, or at soccer.

At home they speak Punjabi with their grandparents, English with their siblings, and something in between with their parents. At school, someone asks about the patka on a boy's head for the hundredth time.

teach.b: The children of Sikh immigrants grow up in two worlds at once. At home: Punjabi, parathas, the Guru Granth Sahib in the front room or a picture of the Gurus on the wall, early morning prayers played from a phone.
Outside: school, friends, sports, a whole other language and way of doing things. Some switch between them without a second thought. Some say they feel pulled in two directions.
Some cut their hair as teenagers, and some of those grow it back later. Some take amrit young.

teach.h: WORKING IT OUT, AT EVERY STAGE.
teach.b: Plenty are still working it out. That's why the weekend Gurmukhi class carries so much weight.
Gurmukhi is the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, and its name is usually explained as from the mouth of the Guru.
Tradition says the second Guru, Guru Angad, shaped and spread it, and taught children to read, so ordinary people could read the Guru's words for themselves.
So the kids tracing letters in Toronto are repeating a lesson tradition says Guru Angad gave the children around him. It's not just a language lesson. It's a key to the Guru.

And the second generation has given something back: Sikh camps, youth groups, podcasts and videos, and a way of explaining the turban, the langar and the Gurus to classmates in the language of the playground.
They carry two worlds. The hope of the weekend class is one heart underneath: the same Guru, the same sangat, just speaking more than one language.

how: Many gurdwaras outside India run weekend Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes, kirtan lessons and youth camps so children can read the Guru Granth Sahib and feel at home in both worlds.

games.q: you're Guru Angad. the Guru's hymns need to reach ordinary people, not just scholars. what does tradition say you did?
o: kept the hymns for trained singers only.
shaped a simple script and taught children to read it.
had the hymns written in Sanskrit.

practice: Choose a word from a language that isn't your main one: one you learned on this path, like sangat or seva, or one a friend or your grandparents taught you.
Say it quietly, and notice how it sits in your mouth, whatever that turns out to be. Then think of someone who lives between two languages every day, and hold them kindly.
